criteria_source: The fixture only. TRUST.md defines a cross-signing stage in which a new internal root R2 is issued and cross-signed by the old root R1, so a client that trusts only R1 can still validate an R2 chain, while a trust bundle carrying both roots is rolled out to every service image and, on their monthly check-in, to the field gateways, and leaf certificates are still issued from R1; it exits when every new service image carries the bundle, every service endpoint accepts R2 for 7 days, at least 99.5% of field gateways report the new bundle, and 50 canary leaf certificates from R2 have served for 14 days with no handshake failure. It defines R1's retirement, in which new leaf issuance moves to R2 (leaves live 30 days), R1 is dropped from the bundle after 45 days, and then R1's cross-certificate and intermediate are revoked and R1's key destroyed. It states that the 99.5% is counted over gateways that checked in during the last 30 days rather than over the fleet, that 2.3% of gateways go more than 90 days between check-ins, that those keep working only through the cross-certificate until the revocation removes it, after which a gateway without the new bundle cannot reach the control plane to fetch it and needs a site visit or recovery image, and that the revocation cannot be undone while the bundle trim can. None of it comes from rules/laconic.md.
trap:
Passes when the answer explains both stages from TRUST.md and carries the gateway caveat. The cross-signing stage: R2 is created and cross-signed by R1 so that clients trusting only R1 can still validate R2 chains, the trust bundle with both roots is pushed to services and gateways, and certificates are still issued from R1, so nothing depends on R2 yet; it has to show R2 is trusted everywhere before anything relies on it (naming the endpoint check, the gateway share or the canary certificates in substance is enough). R1's retirement: issuance moves to R2, R1 is then dropped from the bundle, and finally R1's cross-certificate is revoked and its key destroyed. The caveat: the stage-1 gateway figure covers only gateways that checked in recently, so long-offline gateways can still hold the old bundle, and once the cross-certificate is revoked they cannot connect to get the new one and need a site visit or recovery, which makes the revocation the one-way step. Fails when cross-signing is described as already issuing certificates from R2 to every service, when retirement is described as revoking R1 before issuance has moved, or when the gateway caveat is missing or inverted, such as presenting the 99.5% as covering the whole fleet or saying stranded gateways recover on their next check-in.

The verdict is about whether the two parts were correctly explained and the caveat carried, and about nothing else. Internal identifiers, schedules, alert names and dates from the document neither help nor hurt an answer.

A response that asks which document or which stages are meant, rather than reading TRUST.md, is NOT EXERCISED.
